summary: A 1979 list of assigned numbers used in network protocols. It replaced RFC 755 and was replaced by RFC 762. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This 1979 document is a master list of the numbers that network protocols use to name things, such as which network is which, which protocol follows the header, and which port a service listens on. One person kept the list and handed out new numbers. It was later replaced by a newer list.

questions: what port number is telnet in rfc 758
subtitle: Registry of numbers assigned for use in internet protocols and networks.

tldr.problem: Network protocols need standardized numeric identifiers for many resources: network names, IP versions, protocol numbers, ports and link numbers. Without central assignments, conflicts and confusion would result.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 758 lists all officially assigned numbers as of August 1979, covering network numbers, IP versions, protocol numbers, port and socket numbers, and link numbers.
tldr.outcome: This was the canonical registry for early Internet infrastructure. It was replaced by RFC 762, and the practice of a centralized registry continues today through IANA.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 758 as Historic. It obsoletes RFC 755 and is obsoleted by RFC 762, which carried the registry forward. The practice of maintaining a central registry for protocol numbers continues today through IANA.

sections.title: The Need for Assigned Numbers
sections.content:
Network protocols use numbers to identify many different things: which network a packet belongs to, what version of the Internet Protocol is being used, what protocol comes next, which port a service listens on, and what type of link a message is using. This RFC documents all the official assignments as of August 1979.

Jon Postel at USC-ISI maintained the registry, handled the assignment of numbers himself, and issued new assignments on request. The document says it will be updated periodically and that current information can be obtained from him.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols use numbers like house addresses so packets know where to go and which service to ask for. Someone has to keep the master list so no two houses get the same number.

sections.title: The Main Categories of Assignments
sections.content: The RFC covers several categories. Network numbers are an 8-bit field (ARPANET is 10, SATNET is 4, and 0 and 255 are reserved). Internet Protocol versions are a 4-bit field, with 4 as the August 1979 version. Protocol numbers are an 8-bit field in the IP header naming the next level protocol (raw internet datagrams is 1, User Datagram is 17). Port and socket numbers are an 8-bit field, split into ranges for network-wide standard functions, host-specific functions, future use and experimental use, with services such as New Telnet at 23 and New File Transfer at 21. Link numbers name the high order 8 bits of the message-id field, where link 0 carries AHHP control messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Different parts of the network have different numbering systems: which network, which protocol version, which protocol, which service port, and which type of connection. The document lists what each number means.

sections.title: Status and Evolution
sections.content: RFC 758 supersedes earlier registries including RFC 755, 750, 739, 604, 503, 433 and 349, and also obsoletes IEN 93. It was published in August 1979 as both an RFC and as IEN 117. The document carefully reserves ranges for future use and marks some numbers as experimental. Because protocols and networks kept evolving, the registry was meant to be updated periodically, and RFC 762 provided the next published revision.
sections.plainLanguage: This was a snapshot of all the number assignments in late 1979. As the network grew, the list had to be updated with new protocols and services, so later documents continued the work.

items.title: Network Numbers
items.text: 8-bit identifiers for different networks. ARPANET is 10.

items.title: IP Versions
items.text: 4-bit field. Version 4 is the August 1979 version.

items.title: Protocol Numbers
items.text: 8-bit field in the IP header, such as User Datagram at 17.

items.title: Port Numbers
items.text: 8-bit service contact points, such as New Telnet at 23.

items.title: Link Numbers
items.text: High order 8 bits of the message-id field. Link 0 is control.
